materials.title: COMPSCI 320 Syllabus
pages: COMPSCI 320: Introduction to Software Engineering, Fall 2026. Students learn to build software in teams: requirements, design, testing, version control, continuous integration and code review, through a semester-long team project.
Grading: team project 45% (requirements 10%, milestone 1 10%, milestone 2 10%, final release 15%), labs 20%, quizzes 10%, final exam 25%. Labs are graded by the Gradescope autograder.
Team policy: every team member must contribute code through pull requests. Peer evaluations at each milestone can adjust individual project grades by up to 20%.

materials.title: Lecture 10 slides: Software Testing
pages: Testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence. The goal is to find failures cheaply and early.
Unit tests check one function or class in isolation. Integration tests check that components work together. End-to-end tests drive the whole system like a user.
The test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests.
Coverage: statement coverage counts executed lines; branch coverage counts both outcomes of each decision. High coverage does not mean good tests, but low coverage means untested code.
Test doubles: stubs return canned answers, mocks verify calls, fakes are simple working implementations such as an in-memory database.
Test-driven development: write a failing test, write the smallest code that passes, refactor. Repeat.

materials.title: Lecture 11 slides: Continuous Integration
pages: Continuous integration: every change is merged to the main branch often and checked automatically by a build that runs the tests.
A CI pipeline typically installs dependencies, runs linters, runs unit tests, and reports the result on the pull request before anyone reviews it.
Keep the main branch green. If a change breaks the build, fixing it is the team's top priority.
Flaky tests pass and fail without code changes. Quarantine them and fix the cause; never just re-run until green.

materials.title: Lecture 12 slides: Design Patterns
pages: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common design problems. They give teams a shared vocabulary.
Strategy: put interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the caller can swap them at runtime.
Observer: subjects notify registered observers when their state changes; common in user interfaces.
Adapter: wrap an existing class so it matches the interface a client expects.
Quiz 3 covers Strategy, Observer, Adapter and Factory: know the problem each solves and draw its class diagram.
